summary: Delivery status notifications are limited to ASCII in their machine-readable parts. This RFC adds a new address type for internationalized email addresses so the original recipient with non-ASCII characters is preserved in delivery and disposition notifications.

plainLanguage.summary: When an email bounces, the mail system sends back a report that says what went wrong and which recipient it was for. If the address contains characters outside the plain ASCII set, the older report format cannot carry it, so the sender cannot tell which address the report is about. This document defines new report formats and a new way to write those addresses, so the address survives the round trip.

questions: what is a delivery status notification
how do bounce messages handle non-ascii addresses
what is the utf-8 address type in dsn
subtitle: How bounce and read-receipt messages keep an email address that contains characters outside ASCII.

tldr.problem: Delivery status notifications are limited to ASCII in their machine-readable parts, so an email address with characters outside ASCII cannot be reported back correctly. A client then cannot tell which of its recipients a notification refers to.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a UTF-8 address type with three forms and three new media types, message/global-delivery-status, message/global and message/global-headers, which carry UTF-8 in the parts that used to be 7-bit only.
tldr.outcome: The original recipient is preserved, so notifications can be matched to the recipient the client supplied. This document replaces RFC 5337, which had defined experimental versions of the same media types.

today: RFC 6533 is a Proposed Standard that replaced RFC 5337, which had defined experimental versions of the same media types. The metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Specification Changes
sections.content:
When an email message is transmitted using the SMTPUTF8 extension of RFC 6531 and Internationalized Email Headers of RFC 6532, it is sometimes necessary to return that message or to generate a Message Disposition Notification (MDN) as defined in RFC 3798. A message sent to multiple recipients can generate a status and disposition notification for each recipient, so it helps if a client can correlate these notifications using the recipient address it supplied. Preserving the original recipient is therefore important.

This specification describes how to preserve the original recipient, and updates the MDN and DSN formats to support the new address types.

The document is a revision of and replacement for RFC 5337. While it removes certain constructs from that experimental version, the address type name UTF-8 and the media type names message/global, message/global-delivery-status and message/global-headers have not changed.
sections.plainLanguage: This document fixes the bounce report so that it can carry an email address containing characters outside the plain ASCII set. That lets the sender match each report to the recipient it was about.

sections.title: The UTF-8 Address Type
sections.content:
The address format introduced in Internationalized Email Headers is a new address type for the extensible message format of RFC 3464. An SMTP server that advertises both the SMTPUTF8 extension and the DSN extension of RFC 3461 must accept a UTF-8 address type in the ORCPT parameter, including 8-bit UTF-8 characters.

The address type has three forms: utf-8-addr-xtext, utf-8-addr-unitext and utf-8-address. Only the first form is 7-bit safe. The utf-8-address form holds a native mailbox and is only suitable for protocols that can represent 8-bit characters, so it must not be used in the ORCPT parameter when the server does not advertise SMTPUTF8, when the address contains ASCII characters the ORCPT parameter forbids, such as an unencoded space or the '=' character, or in a 7-bit transport environment such as a message/delivery-status Original-Recipient or Final-Recipient field.

The utf-8-address form may be used in the ORCPT parameter when the server also advertises SMTPUTF8 and the address contains no forbidden ASCII characters. It should be used in a message/global-delivery-status Original-Recipient or Final-Recipient field, and in an Original-Recipient header field when the message is an SMTPUTF8 message. The utf-8-addr-unitext form may be used anywhere the utf-8-address form is allowed.

When the ORCPT parameter is placed in a message/global-delivery-status Original-Recipient field, the utf-8-addr-xtext form should be converted to the utf-8-address form by removing the unitext encoding. An address labelled with the UTF-8 address type that does not conform to utf-8 syntax must be copied into the field without alteration.
sections.plainLanguage: An email address with unusual characters can be written in three ways. One works even on old systems that cannot carry 8-bit characters. Another escapes the awkward characters. The third is the plain address itself and only works where 8-bit characters are allowed.

sections.title: The unitext Encoding
sections.content:
When the UTF-8 address type is used in the ORCPT parameter, ASCII control characters, the space, the backslash, the plus sign and the equals sign must be encoded using the unitext encoding. The unitext encoding uses the syntax \x{HEXPOINT} for encoding any Unicode character outside the ASCII range, and also for encoding the control characters, space, backslash, plus and equals signs. HEXPOINT is 2 to 6 hexadecimal digits.

This encoding avoids the need to use the xtext encoding of RFC 3461, because any ASCII character that would need escaping under xtext never appears in a unitext-encoded string. When sending data to an SMTPUTF8-capable server, native UTF-8 characters should be used instead of the EmbeddedUnicodeChar syntax. When sending data to an SMTP server that does not advertise SMTPUTF8, the EmbeddedUnicodeChar syntax must be used instead of UTF-8.

The document describes the ability to encode characters with the EmbeddedUnicodeChar encodings as a transitional mechanism that should be avoided when possible, in the hope that these encodings can eventually be phased out as systems without SMTPUTF8 support become less common.
sections.plainLanguage: Some characters cannot be written directly in the address field, so they are replaced by a short code that stands for them. A receiving server turns the code back into the original character.

sections.title: The message/global-delivery-status Media Type
sections.content:
A traditional delivery status notification of RFC 3464 comes in a three-part multipart/report container of RFC 6522. The first part is human-readable text describing the error, the second is a 7-bit-only message/delivery-status, and the optional third part returns content (message/rfc822) or headers (text/rfc822-headers). Because the present DSN format does not permit returning an undeliverable SMTPUTF8 message, three new media types have been defined.

The first, message/global-delivery-status, has the syntax of message/delivery-status with three modifications. Its charset is UTF-8, so any field may contain UTF-8 characters when appropriate. In particular the Diagnostic-Code field may contain UTF-8, and should be in the i-default language of RFC 2277. Systems generating the part should use the utf-8-address form for all addresses containing characters outside the ASCII repertoire, and should convert the xtext or unitext form taken from the ORCPT parameter into the utf-8-address form in the Original-Recipient field. Third, an optional Localized-Diagnostic field is added: each instance carries a language tag of RFC 5646 and text in that language, and it is equivalent to the text part of the Diagnostic-Code field. All instances must use different language tags.
sections.plainLanguage: The new report part works like the old one, but its text can hold characters outside the ASCII set. It also has a new field, Localized-Diagnostic, which holds the same message repeated in different languages.

sections.title: Using the New Media Types with multipart/report
sections.content:
As far as a multipart/report container is concerned, message/global-delivery-status, message/global and message/global-headers must be treated as equivalent to message/delivery-status, message/rfc822 and text/rfc822-headers. Implementations processing multipart/report must expect any combination of those six media types inside a multipart/report.

All three new types will typically use the 8bit Content-Transfer-Encoding. If all the content is 7-bit, the equivalent traditional types may be used, for example the message/delivery-status body part when the information in a message/global-delivery-status part can be represented without loss. The document explicitly allows a Content-Transfer-Encoding in message/global-headers and message/global-delivery-status, which MIME had restricted for new message subtypes. This is not believed to be problematic, because the new types are intended mainly for newer systems with full support for 8-bit MIME and UTF-8 headers.

If an SMTP server that advertises both SMTPUTF8 and DSN needs to return an undeliverable SMTPUTF8 message, and the return-path server does not support SMTPUTF8, the undeliverable body part and headers must be encoded with a 7-bit Content-Transfer-Encoding such as base64 or quoted-printable. Otherwise 8bit can be used.
sections.plainLanguage: A report container that used to hold three known part types must now accept three more, and the parser has to handle any mix of the six. The parts that carry 8-bit characters usually travel as 8bit, but on an older network they can be encoded in base64 or quoted-printable instead.

sections.title: UTF-8 Message Disposition Notifications
sections.content:
Message Disposition Notifications of RFC 3798 have a similar design and structure to delivery status notifications, so they use the same basic return format. When an MDN is generated for a UTF-8 header message, the third part of the multipart/report contains the returned content (message/global) or header (message/global-headers), the same as for DSNs.

The second part uses a new media type, message/global-disposition-notification, which has the syntax of message/disposition-notification with two modifications. Its charset is UTF-8, so the failure, error and warning fields may contain UTF-8 characters and should be in the i-default language. Systems generating the part should use the UTF-8 address type for all addresses containing characters outside the ASCII repertoire.

The MDN specification also defines an Original-Recipient header field, which is added with a copy of the contents of ORCPT at delivery time. When generating it, a delivery agent writing a UTF-8 header message in native format should convert the xtext or unitext form of a UTF-8 address type in the ORCPT parameter to the corresponding utf-8-address form. The Disposition-Notification-To header field is an address header field and so follows the same 8-bit rules as other address header fields such as From and To when used in a UTF-8 header message.
sections.plainLanguage: Read receipts and other acknowledgements use the same container as bounce reports, so the same three new part types apply. The fields that carry a human-readable failure or error message can now hold characters outside the ASCII set too.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Automated use of report types without authentication has several security issues. Forging negative reports opens the door to denial-of-service attacks when the reports feed automated maintenance of directories or mailing lists. Forging positive reports may cause the sender to believe a message was delivered when it was not.

Malicious users can generate report structures designed to trigger coding flaws in report parsers. Parsers need secure coding techniques to avoid the risk of buffer overflow or denial-of-service attacks caused by parser mistakes, and code reviews of such parsers are recommended.

Users of the email system regularly send messages with forged envelope return paths, and those messages trigger delivery status reports that produce a large amount of unwanted traffic. Many users therefore ignore delivery status notifications, and never notice when their own messages go undelivered. Supporting correlation of status and disposition notifications with sent messages has become a critical feature of mail clients and possibly mail stores, if the email infrastructure is to remain reliable. In the short term, correlating Message-IDs may be enough to distinguish true status notifications from those resulting from forged originator addresses. In the longer term, including cryptographic signature material that can securely associate the status notification with the original message is advisable.

Because this specification permits UTF-8 in additional fields, the security considerations of UTF-8 in RFC 3629 apply.
sections.plainLanguage: A report can be faked, and a faked failure report can be used to flood a mailing list or a directory. Report parsers also have to be written carefully, because a crafted report is an attack on the software that reads it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The document creates no new IANA registries, but several items were registered as a result of it. The mail address type registry, created by RFC 3464, gained an address type named UTF-8 with the syntax given in Section 3 and the three forms described there. The registration for the 'smtp' diagnostic type was updated to reference this document in addition to RFC 3464 and to drop the reference to RFC 5337; in a message/global-delivery-status body part the codes stay the same, but the text portion may contain UTF-8 characters.

Three media types were registered. For message/global-headers, implementations must not include a charset parameter, because converting the content to another charset would lose information, and the suggested file extension is .u8hdr. For message/global-delivery-status the suggested file extension is .u8dsn, and for message/global-disposition-notification it is .u8mdn. The last two must use the 8-bit content transfer encoding unless they are sent over a 7-bit transport environment, where quoted-printable or base64 may be necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: The new names for these parts and the new address type were written into the official lists, so that no one else uses them for something else.

data.title: utf-8-enc-addr
data.code:
utf-8-enc-addr      = utf-8-addr-xtext /
                         utf-8-addr-unitext /
                         utf-8-address

utf-8-addr-xtext    = 1*(QCHAR / EmbeddedUnicodeChar)

utf-8-addr-unitext  = 1*(QUCHAR / EmbeddedUnicodeChar)

utf-8-address       = Mailbox

EmbeddedUnicodeChar =   %x5C.78 "{" HEXPOINT "}"
